title: What Is Directors & Officers Insurance? D&O Insurance Coverage Guide
summary: What Directors & Officers (D&O) Insurance covers, what it excludes, who needs it, and how cost and limits change as your company raises capital.
body_markdown:
A lead investor asks if you have Directors & Officers (D&O) Insurance before closing your next funding round. Or an independent director wants to know what protection they'll have before joining your board. For most startups, that's when D&O first becomes a priority.


D&O helps protect founders, executives, and board members when they're accused of mismanagement, misleading investors, or breaching their responsibilities to the company. And the stakes can be personal. Without D&O, leadership might have to pay to defend claims involving decisions they made on behalf of the business, even when the allegations turn out to be unfounded.


Understanding what D&O covers, when you need it, and how much protection makes sense can help you put the right policy in place before a contract or funding deadline forces the issue.


## **Key Takeaways**


- D&O protects company leadership. It helps cover certain claims against directors, officers, and executives arising from decisions made on behalf of the business.
- Funding and board formation are common triggers. Many startups purchase D&O when raising outside capital, adding independent directors, or taking on more complex governance responsibilities.
- Costs change as companies grow. Premiums depend on factors like industry, financial condition, capital raised, and coverage limits.
- Claims can arise from major business decisions. Investor disputes, regulatory matters, alleged misrepresentations, and M&A transactions can all create D&O exposure.
- Personal financial exposure is possible. Without adequate coverage or company indemnification, directors and officers may have to fund their own defense or face personal liability for certain claims.


## **What Is Directors & Officers Insurance?**


Directors & Officers (D&O) Insurance helps protect a company's directors, officers, and other covered leaders when they're accused of wrongful acts related to managing the business. These claims may involve alleged mismanagement, breaches of fiduciary duty, misleading statements, or other decisions that cause financial harm.


D&O policies typically include three types of coverage:


1. **Side A:** Protects individual directors and officers when the company can't or isn't permitted to indemnify them, like in certain insolvency situations.
2. **Side B:** Reimburses the company when it pays covered defense costs or other expenses on behalf of its directors and officers.
3. **Side C:** Provides coverage for certain claims against the company itself. The scope varies depending on the policy and whether the company is publicly or privately held.


Together, these protections help address claims against individual leaders and, in certain circumstances, the company itself.


Learn more about the[three sides of D&O Insurance](https://www.vouch.us/blog/sides-a-b-c-directors-and-officers-insurance) .

## **Why Companies Need Directors & Officers Insurance**


Running a company means making decisions that won't always work out as planned. A funding round might fall through, an acquisition might disappoint investors, or a shareholder might question how leadership handled an important financial decision.


Those situations don't automatically lead to lawsuits, but they can create disputes over whether directors and officers fulfilled their responsibilities to the company. And defending those decisions can be expensive, even when leadership ultimately prevails.


The claims that do proceed are getting more expensive:


- The median securities class action settlement rose to[$17 million in 2025, a 10-year high](https://www.nera.com/insights/publications/2026/recent-trends-in-securities-class-action-litigation--2025-full-y.html?lang=en) , even as the number of new filings fell.
- AI is a growing source of claims, with[17 filings in 2025 involving AI-related allegations](https://www.nera.com/insights/publications/2026/recent-trends-in-securities-class-action-litigation--2025-full-y.html?lang=en) , about 8% of all new filings.


For startups, D&O helps provide financial protection when covered allegations arise, allowing leadership to respond without relying entirely on company resources or personal funds.


## **What Directors & Officers Insurance Covers**


D&O Insurance generally helps cover legal defense costs, settlements, and judgments when directors, officers, or other insured parties face claims involving alleged wrongful acts in managing the company.


Common examples include:


- **Investor and shareholder disputes:** Allegations that leadership misrepresented the company's financial condition, valuation, or performance.
- **Breach of fiduciary duty:** Claims that directors or officers failed to act in the company's best interests.
- **Misstatements and reporting errors:** Allegations involving inaccurate financial disclosures or misleading information provided to investors.
- **Regulatory investigations:** Certain investigations or proceedings involving alleged management misconduct, depending on the policy's terms.
- **M&A disputes:** Claims involving disclosures, valuations, or decisions made during an acquisition or other major transaction.


Coverage depends on the policy's definitions, exclusions, and the parties involved in the claim. Not every business dispute or regulatory inquiry will qualify.


Learn more about[what D&O Insurance covers](https://www.vouch.us/blog/what-does-directors-and-officers-insurance-cover) .


## **What Directors & Officers Insurance Doesn't Cover**


D&O Insurance focuses on management-related liability, so it isn't designed to cover every claim your company might face.


Common exclusions or limitations include:


- **Intentional fraud or criminal misconduct:** Policies generally exclude deliberately fraudulent or criminal acts, often subject to a final adjudication requirement.
- **Bodily injury and property damage:** These risks are generally addressed by General Liability Insurance or other applicable liability policies.
- **Professional services errors:** Claims involving mistakes in your company's products or services are typically addressed by Errors & Omissions (E&O) Insurance.
- **Employment-related claims:** Allegations of harassment, discrimination, wrongful termination, or retaliation are generally addressed by[Employment Practices Liability Insurance (EPLI)](https://www.vouch.us/blog/what-does-employment-practices-liability-insurance-cover)


Some claims can involve overlapping allegations, so the circumstances and policy wording determine which coverage may respond.


## **Directors & Officers vs. Other Types of Coverage**


D&O covers how your company is run. Other policies cover what your company does and what happens to it.


Policy Type What It Covers How It Differs From D&O


Errors & Omissions (E&O) Insurance Customer losses caused by errors or failures in your product or service E&O covers what your company does; D&O covers how it's run. See[D&O vs. E&O](https://www.vouch.us/blog/directors-officers-vs-errors-omissions) .


Cyber Insurance Data breaches, ransomware, social engineering, and response costs D&O may respond to certain management-related claims involving cybersecurity oversight.


Crime Insurance Employee theft, funds transfer fraud, forgery, and impersonation D&O doesn't cover theft or fraud committed against the company.


General Liability Insurance Bodily injury, property damage, and advertising injury These risks are generally outside the scope of D&O coverage.


Employment Practices Liability Insurance (EPLI) Harassment, discrimination, wrongful termination, and retaliation claims D&O generally excludes employment practices claims, which are typically addressed by EPLI.


General Partnership Liability (GPL) Personal liability for partners in a general partnership GPL protects partners in a partnership; D&O protects leaders of a corporation or LLC. See[D&O vs. GPL](https://www.vouch.us/blog/directors-officers-vs-general-partnership-liability) .

## **Who Needs Directors & Officers Insurance?**


You don't need to be a large or publicly traded company to face claims involving management decisions. For startups, D&O often becomes relevant when outside investors, board members, or other stakeholders become involved in the business.


Consider purchasing or reviewing D&O coverage when you:


- **Raise outside capital.** Venture and private equity investors frequently require D&O in the term sheet.
- **Add a board, advisors, or board observers.** Independent directors often won't accept a seat without[board member liability coverage](https://www.vouch.us/blog/understanding-board-member-liability-insurance) .
- **Operate in a regulated industry** like fintech, healthcare, or life sciences.
- **Have a complex cap table.** Disputes over valuations, equity, or disclosures are a common source of claims.
- **Prepare for M&A or restructuring.** Decisions made in these moments are frequently challenged after the fact.


If you're approaching one of these milestones, it's worth discussing D&O with your broker before a requirement or potential dispute arises.


## **How Much Does Directors & Officers Insurance Cost?**


D&O Insurance costs depend on your company's financial condition, industry, funding history, governance structure, and coverage limits.


Capital raised is an important consideration because new funding can change a company's valuation, investor expectations, and potential exposure to claims. As a result, D&O premiums may increase after a funding round, although the impact varies by company and insurer.


According to Vouch's D&O pricing data, the median premium is approximately $6,000 per year. Companies that have raised less than $2M typically pay closer to $3,300 to $3,900 annually. Your board composition, claims history, retention, and selected coverage limits can also influence pricing.


Learn more about[how much D&O Insurance costs](https://www.vouch.us/blog/directors-and-officers-insurance-cost) .


## **How Much Directors & Officers Insurance Do You Need?**


The right D&O limit depends on your company's stage, investor expectations, board structure, and potential exposure to management-related claims.


Early-stage startups often begin with $1M in coverage, but that amount may need to increase as the company raises capital, adds board members, or prepares for a major transaction.


When choosing a limit, consider your funding history, the number of individuals who need protection, and the potential cost of defending a significant claim. It's also worth reviewing whether your policy includes adequate Side A protection for individual directors and officers.


Learn more about[how much D&O Insurance you need](https://www.vouch.us/blog/how-much-directors-and-officers-insurance-do-i-need) .

## **Directors & Officers Insurance Claims Examples**


D&O claims can arise when investors, regulators, or other stakeholders question how company leadership handled an important decision.


Here are three examples of situations where coverage might apply.


### **1. Alleged Investor Misrepresentation**


Say a startup raises capital after presenting financial projections to investors. When the company misses those projections, an investor alleges that leadership knowingly misrepresented its financial condition.


D&O may help cover the resulting defense costs and any covered settlement, depending on the policy's terms.


### **2. Regulatory Investigation**


Say a financial services company receives a regulatory inquiry involving disclosures made by senior leadership. The company hires legal counsel to respond to document requests and investigate the allegations.


Certain D&O policies may cover eligible defense or investigation costs, depending on the scope of coverage.


### **3. Acquisition Dispute**


Say a startup is acquired, but the buyer later alleges that leadership withheld material information during negotiations. The buyer files a claim against the company's former directors and officers.


D&O may respond to certain covered allegations, subject to policy exclusions and any applicable transaction-related provisions.


## **Protect Your Leadership as Your Company Grows**


The decisions founders and executives make today can create liability long after a funding round closes or a board meeting ends. D&O Insurance helps protect the people making those decisions when covered claims arise.


If you're raising outside capital, adding directors, or preparing for a major transaction, it's worth reviewing your coverage before those milestones arrive. A Vouch advisor can help you evaluate your D&O needs and find coverage that fits your company's stage and plans for growth.


## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### **Is Directors & Officers Insurance required by law?**


Generally, D&O isn't designed to cover ordinary operational incidents like customer service failures, bodily injuries, or property damage. Those risks are typically addressed by E&O, General Liability, or other applicable policies. However, an operational incident could also lead to a separate management-related claim, depending on the circumstances.


### **Does Directors & Officers Insurance cover the company or just individuals?**


Both. Side A protects individuals when the company can't indemnify them, while Side B and Side C apply to the company.


### **Do early-stage companies really need Directors & Officers Insurance?**


Many do. Claims often arise during fundraising, founder departures, cap table disputes, or early partnerships, all of which happen well before profitability.


### **How do you get Directors & Officers Insurance?**


Start before your round closes, since investors often require it and rates typically rise after a raise. Underwriters will ask for your financials, cap table, and board details, so it helps to know[what the D&O underwriting process involves](https://www.vouch.us/blog/directors-and-officers-insurance-underwriting) .


### **Does Directors & Officers Insurance cover operational incidents?**


No. Injuries, property damage, and service errors fall under policies like General Liability Insurance or E&O Insurance.


### **Is Directors & Officers Insurance "set and forget"?**


No. Reassess your limits annually and at major milestones like a fundraise, expansion, leadership change, or entry into a regulated market.


### **Does D&O Insurance apply to LLCs, or only to corporations?**


D&O applies to LLCs, C corps, and S corps. Coverage is tied to leadership roles and decisions, not corporate structure, so it's worth evaluating if your LLC has outside investors or a managing board.


### **What's the difference between a retention and a deductible in a D&O policy?**


A retention is the amount the insured must pay toward a covered claim before the insurer begins paying applicable costs. A deductible serves a similar purpose, although the mechanics can differ by policy. Retentions generally don't reduce the stated policy limit, but defense expenses and other covered payments may.


### **What happens to my D&O coverage when my company is acquired?**


A change of control typically triggers runoff provisions in a D&O policy, meaning the existing coverage generally applies only to alleged wrongful acts that occurred before the acquisition. Companies often purchase extended reporting coverage, commonly called[D&O tail coverage](https://www.vouch.us/blog/understanding-tail-insurance) , to allow claims involving those past decisions to be reported after the transaction.[Six-year tail periods are common](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2021-may/what-you-should-know/) , although the appropriate terms depend on the deal and policy.
